title: Red Allen, Buster Bailey and the friends who have died
summary: Moore reflects on his friendship with Red Allen and Buster Bailey and lists those who died, and the jazz clubs he visited while with Lanin.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Very interesting, very exciting time that you've had there.
Even you're getting a kick out of it.

Okay, during the time that you were at at the Stuyvesant Casino you also played as evidenced by that bootleg recording with Buster Bailey, of course that was with the Henry Red Allen group. How was Buster? You're pretty fond of his music.

Yes -- I should say at this point that when I was with Lester Lanin I always thought of my nights at the Stuyvesant Casino and the Central Plaza and wondering how the boys are doing and I was quite busy with Lester. But my memory always returned to the different guys I was close to. And the fellas that I was very close to during them years was Buster Bailey and Red Allen because we spent so much time in the Metropole together and it used to be that every time I'd come in from the street into the Metropole, Red would stop and he'd announce me, it wouldn't be he'd say my birthday but / here's a trombone player who is a great trombonist and today is his birthday" -- it wouldn't be my birthday but Red would always put me on --"today's

his birthday -- how about saying hello to Big Chief, Russell Moore," he'd say. It always knocked me out. I must tell you, going back just a little bit at the time I was contracted to play Georgetown in Washington at Blues Alley. I was with Tom Gwaltney's band, I was there as a guest and I spent about two weeks there and one night, all night long, we were wailing and then at the end of the night Tom Gwaltney says, "I want to see you at the office." So I said to myself, what did I do this time. I'm going to be fired or they're letting me go or something. So I'm up there now in the office with Tom Gwaltney, the clarinet player, he had a band, nice band. So I went up there with him, "Sit down, I didn't want to tell you this Chief," he said. Now I'm alarmed. "While you were performing downstairs I get a call from New York that Red Allen died and I couldn't tell you while you were performing." I said, "I can't believe it." He had passed away. I don't remember what year that was that Red passed away but that's one of the stories that was sad to relate. When you're in this business you never know who's going to go because many of those people that I worked with at Central Plaza as of this time

You know, Louis got a recording "By and By," and in the song the lyrics have been changed to fit the times, depicting the jazz musicians that have gone and in the song he talks about Jack Jenny being up there, up in heaven --
And 3ig Sid Catlett. It's a beautiful rendition of that, I'd like to take that and keep it for my file always.
